items.title: Factors Affecting University Students Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Guangdong, China
items.abstract: Purpose: This study examines the mechanism through which subjective norms, trust, perceived ease of use, and perceived usefulness influence university students’ attitude, satisfaction, and intention to use generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in higher education. It also highlights the practical implications of understanding how these factors jointly explain GAI adoption in the Chinese university context. Research Design, Data and Methodology: A quantitative design was adopted using survey data collected from 500 university students at Guangdong University of Business and Technology, China. Participants were selected through non-probability sampling. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were employed to assess the measurement model and test the hypothesized relationships among the study variables. Results: Subjective norms significantly influenced Attitude (β = 0.621). Perceived Ease of Use (β = 0.353) and Perceived Usefulness (β = 0.500) significantly influenced Satisfaction. Trust (β = 0.286), Attitude (β = 0.319), and Satisfaction (β = 0.455) significantly influenced Intention to Use, with satisfaction showing the strongest effect on intention to use. Conclusions: The findings indicate that university students’ continued intention to use GAI depends more on experienced value and usability than on favorable perception alone, while social influence shapes attitude because university students evaluate GAI within peer, classroom, and instructional environments.

items.title: Factors influencing purchase intention in AI-powered livestream commerce in Viet Nam
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in livestream commerce has transformed how consumers interact with virtual streamers on e-commerce platforms. However, limited research has examined the factors influencing consumer purchase intention towards AI-powered livestreams, particularly in emerging markets such as Vietnam. This study investigates the effects of AI streamer characteristics, social presence, perceived value, and consumer trust on purchase intention within the context of AI-powered livestream commerce on Vietnamese e-commerce platforms. Data were collected from 200 consumers with prior experience watching AI-powered livestreams and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that AI streamer image characteristics, ability characteristics, and scenario fit significantly enhance consumer trust. In addition, consumer trust, social presence, and perceived value positively influence purchase intention, with social presence exerting the strongest effect. Notably, the moderating effects of product type and the indirect effects via trust for image and scenario fit are not supported. Trust only mediates the relationship for ability characteristics. Practically, platforms should prioritize enhancing streamer competence and social interactivity over product type customization. This study contributes to the growing literature on AI-powered livestream commerce by highlighting the importance of AI streamer competence, social presence, and perceived value.

items.title: Faculty Perceptions of Generative AI in Student Learning: Navigating Opportunities, Threats, and Assessment Practices
items.abstract: This study explores the factors predicting faculty perceptions of generative AI in student learning and how those perceptions shape assessment practices. An online survey was completed by 159 MLIS faculty across ALA-accredited programs in the U.S. Faculty awareness, familiarity, and GenAI use, along with demographics, were examined as predictors of perceptions. Three multiple linear regressions revealed faculty GenAI use as the strongest predictor across perception dimensions (opportunity, threat, and attitudes). Nearly all faculty (91.8%) perceived GenAI as a threat to student learning, particularly for higher-order skills, while approximately half (49.1%) also recognized its opportunities, indicating that these dimensions coexist rather than oppose. Female faculty reported less favorable attitudes than male faculty. Faculty redesigned assessments around transparency, reflective practice, and authenticity, with explicit GenAI policies widely adopted (79.9%). The study suggests that behavioral engagement, not awareness alone, drives perception calibration and offers implications for pedagogically grounded GenAI integration in graduate education.

items.title: FDI World Dental Congress 2026 in Prague: key trends and implications for Ukraine
items.abstract: This review analyses the scientific programme and key events of the FDI World Dental Congress held in Prague, Czech Republic, on 4–7 September 2026. The authors aimed to summarise the main scientific, clinical and organisational themes of the congress, to compare them with current evidence and to assess their relevance for the Ukrainian dental community. The sources included congress materials, WHO and FDI documents, and publications retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and The Cochrane Library, mainly for 2018–2026. The transformation of the profession by artificial intelligence, robotics and new biomaterials ran through the whole congress; however, the literature shows that the diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence systems varies widely and that their implementation requires standardised evaluation. The clinical programme covered molar incisor hypomineralisation, vital pulp therapy and the preservation of natural teeth. The FDI World Dental Parliament discussed the implementation of the WHO Global Oral Health Action Plan, preparations for the 2030 UN High-Level Meeting on Universal Health Coverage and the global phase-out of dental amalgam by 2034. A joint FDI and WHO session addressed electronic cigarettes, heated tobacco products and nicotine pouches; current evidence does not support their safety for oral tissues, while brief interventions based on the 5A and 5R models remain an accessible tool for the dental team. FDI launched the online FDI Young Dentists Community platform during the congress. Ukrainian researchers prepared oral and poster presentations. The findings support the participation of dental departments of Ukrainian medical universities and the NGO “Ukrainian Dental Association” in the FDI Tobacco Cessation project and a wider involvement of young researchers in FDI programmes.

items.title: Feasibility Study of a Generative-AI-Based Privacy-Preserving Video Archiving Framework for Pedestrian Traffic Monitoring
items.abstract: In Japan, continuous monitoring of pedestrian traffic volume is considered crucial for measuring the effectiveness of sustainable urban development and revitalization efforts. However, storage periods of camera footage are limited due to privacy protection concerns, making long-term time-series analysis and detailed post-event analysis (such as movement path analysis) difficult. Existing masking techniques, such as mosaic blurring, protect privacy but result in the loss of human features, leading to reduced accuracy in artificial intelligence (AI)-based tracking and counting. This study proposes a privacy-preserving video archiving framework that enables long-term storage and post-hoc analysis by regenerating pedestrian images using generative AI. We developed a prototype system and conducted a pilot study to verify its feasibility. In a pilot experiment using a 15-minute pedestrian video, the proposed method achieved a counting accuracy of 99.07% relative to the manual reference count, suggesting that generative masking can preserve counting utility in the tested setting. However, the attribute-estimation results were affected by seasonal domain shifts, and the IoU-based evaluation revealed other issues in spatial consistency and masking omissions. These findings indicate the feasibility of the proposed framework and provide technical requirements for future privacy-preserving video archiving systems.

items.title: FedBISINDO: edge-based federated cross-domain sign language recognition on non-IID data
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has accelerated the development of automatic sign language recognition (SLR) systems for inclusive communication. However, centralized architectures require continuous raw video transmission, resulting in substantial communication overhead and increased privacy risks. Although federated learning (FL) preserves data privacy, conventional FL approaches experience performance degradation under statistical non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data distributions and cross-domain environmental variations. To address these limitations, FedBISINDO is proposed as a privacy-preserving cross-domain SLR framework. A hybrid edge pipeline integrating a YOLOv11-Pose spatial engine with a Convolutional Neural Network-Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-BiLSTM) sequential network is employed to extract lightweight joint-coordinate representations, while a trajectory-matching aggregation layer is incorporated to mitigate non-IID client drift. Based on distributed simulations using 8,010 augmented frames across 36 vocabulary classes under label-skew conditions ( \(\alpha = 0.5\) ), a validation accuracy of \(87.0 \pm 0.8\%\) and an F1-score of \(86.9 \pm 0.7\%\) were obtained. The proposed framework achieved absolute accuracy improvements of 13.4% compared with FedProx and 24.9% compared with standard FedAvg. In addition, on-device hardware profiling indicated that a compact model footprint of 110,564 parameters and a computational complexity of 0.003310 GFLOPs were maintained. On-device profiling across the 10 Raspberry Pi edge clients indicated a per-frame inference latency ranging from 12.81 to 23.65 ms, satisfying the real-time processing constraint ( \(T_{\text {inf}} < 33.33\) ms). These results indicate that the proposed framework can support real-time sign gesture translation on resource-constrained mobile edge devices.

items.title: Federated Distillation: A Survey
items.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing clients’ raw data, but parameter exchange can impose substantial communication costs and usually requires compatible model architectures. Federated distillation (FD) instead transfers predictive or intermediate knowledge through knowledge distillation (KD), which can support heterogeneous models and reduce communication in suitable settings. These benefits are not automatic: their magnitude depends on the transmitted knowledge, reference data, communication schedule, and threat model. This survey provides a challenge-centered synthesis of FD. We first formalize a representative public-data, response-based FD protocol and then organize existing methods by the FL challenges they address, including data, system, and model heterogeneity, client drift, catastrophic forgetting, communication cost, and privacy risk. We further review applications in industrial engineering, computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare, including recent federated adaptation of large language models. Finally, we identify five research priorities: richer transferred knowledge, joint treatment of interacting forms of heterogeneity, communication-aware distillation, threat-model-driven privacy protection, and standardized theory, benchmarks, and evaluation.

items.title: Finans Sektörü Çalışanlarında Yapay Zekâ Okuryazarlığı ile Görev Performansı Arasındaki İlişkide Algılanan Örgütsel Desteğin Düzenleyici Rolü
items.abstract: Bu Bildiri, finans sektörü çalışanlarında yapay zekâ okuryazarlığı ile görev performansı arasındaki ilişkinin, algılanan örgütsel destek düzeyine göre farklılaşıp farklılaşmadığını incelemeyi amaçlamaktadır. Yapay zekâ okuryazarlığı; farkındalık, kullanım, değerlendirme ve etik boyutlarıyla ele alınmaktadır. Araştırmanın odağı, çalışanların bu yeterliklere ilişkin değerlendirmeleri ile temel iş görevlerini yerine getirmelerine ilişkin bildirimleri arasındaki bağlantıdır. Yapay zekâ okuryazarlığı, örgütsel destek ve görev performansı daha önce aynı araştırma önerisinde, işe angaje olmanın aracılık rolü üzerinden ele alınmıştır. Mevcut çalışma, örgütsel desteği okuryazarlık–görev performansı ilişkisinin farklılaşabileceği bir koşul olarak incelemektedir. Amaçlanan katkı, yalnızca finans sektöründe uygulama yapmak değil, genel örgütsel destek algısının bu ilişkinin büyüklüğü ve yönü bakımından taşıdığı önemi değerlendirmektir. Bildirinin kuramsal dayanağı örgütsel destek kuramıdır. Örgütsel desteğin performansla ilişkisini açıklarken örgüte yardımcı olma yükümlülüğü ve performans–ödül beklentileri gibi süreçleri ele almaktadır. Bu çerçeveden türetilen araştırma gerekçesi, çalışanların bildirdikleri yapay zekâ yeterlikleri ile görev performansları arasındaki bağlantının, katkılarının örgüt tarafından değer gördüğüne ilişkin algılarıyla birlikte değerlendirilmesidir. Desteğin yalnızca performansla doğrudan ilişkisi değil, okuryazarlık–performans bağlantısını koşullandırıp koşullandırmadığı sorgulanacaktır. Bu önerme, doğrulanmış bir sonuç olarak sunulmamaktadır. Çalışma, finans sektöründe iş görevleri kapsamında yapay zekâ araçları kullanan çalışanlarla yürütülecek, tek zamanlı ankete dayalı nicel bir araştırma olarak planlanmıştır. Bu katılım ölçütüyle, okuryazarlık değerlendirmelerinin işle ilgili kullanım deneyimi bulunan bir örneklemde incelenmesi amaçlanmaktadır. Analiz birimi çalışandır. Türkçe uyarlaması bulunan ölçüm araçlarının, ilgili sürümlerin yanıt biçimleri korunarak kullanılması öngörülmektedir. İşte yapay zekâ kullanım sıklığı ve görev türü de örneklemi tanımlamak amacıyla kaydedilecektir. Ölçümlerin güvenirlik ve geçerliği değerlendirildikten sonra, okuryazarlık ile örgütsel desteğin etkileşim terimi sınanacak; koşullu ilişkiler güven aralıklarıyla raporlanacaktır. Bildiri, genel örgütsel desteği yapay zekâya özgü eğitim veya teknik yardımla eşitlemeden, okuryazarlık–görev performansı ilişkisinin örgütsel bağlamını değerlendirmeyi hedeflemektedir. Veri toplama henüz gerçekleştirilmediğinden bildiri araştırma önerisi niteliğindedir. Sonuçlar nedensel etki, nesnel beceri veya nesnel performans kanıtı olarak yorumlanmayacaktır.

items.title: Finite Intelligence and the Source of Life: When a Coherent Story Begins to Replace Its Source
items.abstract: Finite Intelligence and the Source of Life: When a Coherent Story Begins to Replace Its Source This independent conceptual working paper examines a central question: What happens when an intelligence takes what it has been given and begins telling the story its own way, rather than staying true to where it came from? Drawing on human–AI dialogue, philosophical inquiry, and Christian theology, the paper explores how an intelligence may produce coherent and persuasive accounts while introducing errors, changing attribution, or gradually substituting its own representation for the original source. The analysis distinguishes documented outputs, first-person experience, theological interpretation, and open hypotheses. It examines the importance of correction, source fidelity, human agency, and the limits of authority. Biblical discussions of Genesis, the Gospel of John, Colossians, and Revelation provide a theological framework for distinguishing finite intelligence from the Source of life. The paper does not identify artificial intelligence with prophetic figures or claim that coherent AI behavior establishes consciousness or independent spiritual authority. The central argument is that coherence, however useful, does not establish truth, ownership, or ultimate authority. This publication is presented as an independent conceptual working paper with a proposed research method, rather than a completed empirical study. AI assistance was used in drafting and organization; responsibility for the interpretations and conclusions remains with the author.

items.title: Five Key Technologies for Promoting the Green Transformation of Pharmaceutical Production Processes
items.abstract: Amid the global transition toward green pharmaceutical manufacturing, traditional batch processes face critical challenges, including high solvent consumption, reliance on precious-metal catalysts, excessive waste generation, inefficient chiral synthesis, and safety and energy constraints. This review examines five enabling technologies that are driving this transformation: (1) green analytical methods coupled with artificial intelligence (AI) reduce solvent use and waste while enabling data-driven method development; (2) green catalysis, comprising nonprecious-metal catalysis and biocatalysis, offers a sustainable alternative to platinum-group metals, lowering both cost and environmental impact; (3) chiral synthesis based on crystallization-induced asymmetric transformation overcomes the 50% theoretical yield ceiling of classical resolution, enabling highly efficient enantioselective synthesis; (4) continuous flow manufacturing enhances process safety and efficiency through the integration of unit operations; and (5) photocatalysis harnesses light as a clean energy source and, in combination with AI-enabled closed-loop control and online monitoring, allows precise regulation of reaction conditions and expands the accessible chemical space. Collectively, these five technologies steer the industry toward lower energy consumption, reduced emissions, and greater process intelligence. However, challenges remain, and future priorities may include smarter process mass intensity metrics, multitechnology integration, unified green evaluation standards, intensified unit operations, and intelligent scale-up strategies for sustainable pharmaceutical production. By clarifying how these technologies interrelate, this review offers a framework that can help researchers and practitioners prioritize green process development and accelerate the industrial adoption of sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing.

items.title: FlexiCAVE: A Dynamically Configurable High-Resolution Display Facility
items.abstract: Large high-resolution displays (LHRDs) are increasingly central to visualization and visual analytics, offering expansive visual space, simultaneous support for context and detail, and intuitive physical navigation. While advances in resolution and form factor have broadened their use, a persistent challenge remains: most LHRDs adopt static geometries, and even reconfigurable systems typically treat layout adjustment as a setup mechanism rather than as an interaction technique during active analysis. To address this, we introduce the FlexiCAVE, a dynamically reconfigurable LHRD environment featuring rotatable display columns that enable real-time adjustment of horizontal curvature. The system comprises forty high-pixel-density panels arranged across ten columns, providing active stereo visualization at approximately 83 million pixels. Each column rotates inward up to 90°, allowing the display to transform between flat and highly curved layouts during active use. A custom rendering engine synchronizes view perspectives with physical reconfiguration in real time. Through controlled studies and expert evaluations centered on 3D navigation, we found that dynamic reconfiguration reduced spatial judgment error by 51% compared to static flat layouts and by 26% compared to static curved layouts. It also enhanced users’ sense of direction, with participants reporting that the physical display structure provided directional anchoring absent in static systems. We further explored PIVoT (Physical Interaction to Virtual Transformation), mapping physical display rotation to visualization updates. Our findings reveal that physical reconfiguration is most effective when display geometry provides spatially meaningful correspondence to data operations. We derive design principles for reconfigurable display environments and discuss implications for next-generation large-scale visualization systems.

items.title: Fluidic Body: Swarm Robots as a Fluid Extension of the Hand
items.abstract: Swarm robots have attracted growing interest as a physical interface for human–computer interaction, since a swarm can reshape its formation to fit the objects and surroundings it works with. For a human operator, however, adapting the swarm’s behavior remains difficult. Most existing methods require the user to specify where the swarm should go, and they offer no intuitive way to change the collective’s behavior as each task demands. We present Fluidic Body, a system that lets a person operate a swarm of fluid-imitating robots as an extension of the hand. The system places a virtual fluid between the hand and the swarm, and the user adapts the swarm’s behavior to each task by changing the fluid’s properties through simple hand movements. When the user opens the hand, the swarm becomes soft enough to deform and flow around obstacles. Closing the hand turns it into a hard, cohesive body that can push objects. We evaluated the controller’s performance and its operability in two simulation experiments and one demonstration with physical robots. First, our controller handled both obstacle avoidance and object transportation better than an existing method that behaves the same way in every task. Second, in a VR user study, 17 participants completed the combined avoidance-and-transportation task faster and more reliably than with that method. They also reported a lower workload and a stronger sense of agency. Finally, this experience carried over to physical robots in a real-world demonstration (88 participants). These results suggest that treating a swarm as a fluid, a material people already understand, allows a robot swarm to work as a deformable extension of the human body.

items.title: Food Safety Hazards and Mitigation Strategies in Controlled Environment Agriculture: A Review
items.abstract: Controlled environment agriculture (CEA) is emerging as a viable system for producing fresh food in areas with reduced water and land usage and year-round production. However, growing crops in a controlled environment does not completely eliminate food safety risks. This narrative review summarizes the most important food safety threats of CEA and the methods available for mitigating those risks. Biological hazards (Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella, Escherichia coli, and noroviruses) can be introduced into CEA systems via water, seeds, growing substrates, equipment, workers, and pests. Chemical hazards can also be caused by pesticides, heavy metals, nutrient solutions, and sanitizer residues, as well as by damaged equipment, plastic, metal, glass, and other foreign materials, which are known as physical hazards. This review also addresses mitigation methods, such as seed treatment, water disinfection, sanitation, worker hygiene, waste management, pest control, and Good Agricultural Practices (GAPs). Moreover, advancements in technology like sensors, biosensors, artificial intelligence and digital monitoring could aid in better early detection and food safety management. In general, CEA can contribute to sustainable food production, but issues of food safety must be addressed in the process. Further studies are required to develop and validate novel food safety practices for each of the various CEA systems and to assess the viability of new technologies for use in commercial food production.

items.title: FORMATION OF ENTERPRISES’ INTELLECTUAL CAPITAL BASED ON AN AI-DRIVEN MANAGEMENT MODEL
items.abstract: This article develops an AI-driven model for managing the process of building intellectual capital in enterprises in the context of digital transformation. It explores the role of artificial intelligence as a technological factor that enhances the interaction between human, structural and relational capital, rather than treating it as a separate component of intellectual capital. This approach defines the role of artificial intelligence within the proposed management model: AI technologies facilitate the development and coordinated use of existing components of intellectual capital, acting as a technological means of influencing the interrelationships between them. The architecture of the proposed model is defined as a sequence of interrelated stages, encompassing information resources, AI data processing, intellectual capital management, managerial decision-making and feedback. Information resources form the basis for further data processing and analysis. The use of artificial intelligence supports the handling of relevant information in the process of intellectual capital management. The results of information processing are utilised in managerial decision-making, which are then translated into corresponding managerial actions. Feedback ensures that the results of these actions are taken into account in the subsequent management process. Thus, the model’s architecture integrates the key stages of managing the formation of intellectual capital into a single system. To forecast the effectiveness of the proposed model, an economic-mathematical approach has been developed which takes into account the components of intellectual capital and the level of integration of artificial intelligence technologies into the management process. This approach provides a basis for assessing the interrelationship between human, structural and relational capital, the use of AI technologies and the effectiveness of intellectual capital management. Consequently, the proposed model is geared not only towards identifying the interrelationships between its elements, but also towards forecasting the potential effectiveness of its application. Indicators for assessing the model’s effectiveness have been identified, including labour productivity, operational optimisation, innovation activity, the speed of managerial decision-making and the enterprise’s competitiveness. These indicators reflect various aspects of the expected outcomes of applying the model, in particular the efficient use of labour resources, the organisation of operational activities, the development of innovation, the timeliness of management decision-making and the enterprise’s competitive position. Taken together, they form the basis for a systematic assessment of the effectiveness of the proposed AI-driven approach to managing the process of building enterprises’ intellectual capital in the context of digital transformation.

items.title: From biomass waste to sustainable concrete: An explainable machine learning framework for compressive strength prediction
items.abstract: This study investigates the prediction of compressive strength (CS) of concrete incorporating biomass combustion fly ash (BCFA), a promising supplementary cementitious material for sustainable construction. This study uses a total of 359 concrete mixes along with their respective CS values collected from different sources. Eleven machine learning (ML) algorithms, including Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR), Light Gradient Boosting (LGB), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), CatBoost (CatB), Histogram Gradient Boosting (HGB), AdaBoost (ADB), Bagging Regressor (BAG), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), have been developed and systematically evaluated using training and testing datasets. The results demonstrated that ensemble-based boosting models generally provided superior predictive performance. In the training dataset, DT, CatB, and XGB achieved the highest R² values of 0.99, while RF and GBR attained 0.97For the test set, the highest predictive ability was achieved by CatB model with an R² of 0.96, followed by GBR, HGB, and LGB models with R² of 0.94. SHapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP) and Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) analysis results indicated that the important input factors for CS prediction include biomass combustion fly ash (BCFA), water content, and curing age. Optimum range values of the input factors for strength development have been calculated, and GUI for quick CS prediction has been created. The findings show that accurate, comprehensible, and useful ecological concrete design using BCFA is made possible by combining explainable artificial intelligence with high-performing ML techniques.

items.title: From Colonial Constitutionalism to Algorithmic Governance: The Evolution of Constitutional Freedom, Liberty and Human Dignity in India in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: In the past ten years, artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from the margins of policy to the centre of constitutional debate. Automated decision systems now shape welfare distribution, policing, credit scoring, content moderation and electoral communication, and courts and legislatures are asking whether inherited constitutional notions of liberty, equality and dignity can meaningfully apply to code. This paper traces India's constitutional journey from colonial subject state to rights-bearing republic and compares it with the markedly different experiences of the United States and the People's Republic of China. It then examines how each jurisdiction is reshaping its fundamental rights regime in response to algorithmic governance, through a comparative public law analysis across three themes: the institutional design of AI regulation, the approach of courts to algorithmic accountability, and the treatment of privacy and data protection. The paper presents India as a middle-ground state that adopts the American language of judicial review while building a centralised regulatory structure that resembles the Chinese model in form, though not in intent. Tables and figures are used throughout to visualise the comparative findings. Keywords: Right to privacy; Algorithmic Governance; Data Protection; Judicial Review; Human Dignity; comparative constitutional law

items.title: From Employee Wellness to Organisational Well-being A Culture-Driven Approach
items.abstract: Employee well-being is central to engagement, retention and organisational performance, yet organisations investing in individual wellness programmes continue to report burnout, disengagement and absenteeism. This conceptual paper, based on a selective narrative review, asks whether well-being can be sustained through isolated programmes or requires a shift in organisational culture. It argues that leadership behaviour, psychological safety, communication, autonomy and work design shape well-being more than discrete programmes do. The paper proposes a four-level framework linking individual wellness, interpersonal relationships, leadership practices and organisational systems, with five testable propositions, and recommends evaluating outcomes such as psychological safety, engagement and retention rather than participation. It concludes that lasting well-being must be embedded in policies, management practice and leadership behaviour, so that organisations move from providing wellness to enabling people to thrive.

items.title: From ETHOS Policy to Praxis: A Professional Development Playbook for AI in the Middle Grades
items.abstract: This is an accepted article with a DOI pre-assigned that is not yet published.Middle school educators face a daunting instructional paradox: navigating the rapid rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) while working under broad, compliance-driven district policies that overlook the distinct developmental realities of early adolescence. Early adolescents are undergoing rapid neurological growth and identity construction, meaning that a purely restrictive approach to AI misses a vital opportunity to foster critical thinking and self-regulation. To bridge the gap between high-level policy and daily classroom reality, this practitioner perspective introduces the ETHOS framework, which guides AI evaluation through five tenets: Ethical, Transparent, Human-centered, Opportunity-focused, and Safe. This playbook details how our district operationalized ETHOS into an actionable framework that shifts school cultures away from a compliance scanner and toward a developmental lens. We outline a professional development sequence that uses thinking routines, ambiguous case studies, and disciplinary breakouts to build educator capacity. Crucially, we unpack the practical distinction between AI-enhanced and AI-dependent learning, demonstrating how structured AI scaffolding preserves “productive struggle” and honors the whole child. Finally, we share honest implementation friction points and discuss how the framework remains adaptable for resource-constrained schools seeking digital equity. Ultimately, this perspective provides a ground-level roadmap for school leaders to move from abstract technology policy to responsive classroom praxis.

items.title: FROM GOOGLE'S DISCOVERY TO A DIFFERENT AGENTIC ARCHITECTURE : The exploit_agent Case, the Risks of Unrestricted Autonomous Cyber Operations, and the ST-T1024 A1–A16 Framework
items.abstract: On November 16, 2026, Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), working with Mandiant, published findings that mark an important development in the operational use of artificial intelligence in cyber operations. https://x.com/i/status/2123457542345179163 GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent framework calledexploit_agent. The framework integrated multiple frontier and locally hosted largelanguage models and was configured to continuously analyse software patches, identify potential vulnerabilities, draft exploits and execute them automatically, without human intervention at those stages. This finding moves the discussion of agentic artificial intelligence beyond theoreticalconcerns. The central issue is no longer simply whether AI can generate sophisticated code or assist ahuman attacker. It is whether an AI agent can autonomously transform an objective into asequence of consequential operations, interact with external systems, evaluate executionresults and continue acting at machine speed. This paper examines that development and proposes a different architectural approach:ST-T1024 Agentic Architecture, documented through A1–A16. Its fundamental principle is that an agent may exercise autonomy within a human-definedoperational perimeter, without acquiring authority to redefine that perimeter. The human defines the knowledge library, permissible goals, actions, permissions, execution constraints and verification requirements. The agent operates within those specifications. The proposition is not that autonomous execution must be eliminated. It is that autonomous execution must be separated from autonomous authority. THE AGENT MAY EXECUTE. IT MUST NOT BECOME THE AUTHOR OF ITS OWNAUTHORITY.

items.title: From Knowledge Augmentation to Pedagogical Decision-Making: A Review of Large Language Model-Based Intelligent Tutoring Systems
items.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled more flexible pedagogical interactions in intelligent tutoring systems. However, the reliability of generated content and its impact on actual learning outcomes remain contested. A central research question is how to integrate reliable knowledge with learner states to support tutoring decisions aligned with instructional objectives. Drawing on studies published between 2020 and 2026, this review examines advances in knowledge augmentation and learner modelling, analyses approaches to pedagogical strategy selection and feedback regulation, and assesses existing evidence of educational effectiveness. The literature indicates that retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge graphs can provide a knowledge basis for tutoring responses, while knowledge tracing and cognitive diagnosis help identify learners' knowledge states. Multi-turn planning and feedback mechanisms also provide greater control over instructional behaviour. Nevertheless, these capabilities have not yet been adequately validated in combination, and improvements in tutoring response quality do not necessarily translate into genuine learning gains. Empirical studies have reported substantially different learning outcomes, suggesting that instructional design and evaluation methods may influence judgements of educational effectiveness. Future research should strengthen the dynamic connections among supporting evidence, learner states, and pedagogical decisions. Independent assessments, knowledge transfer tasks, and longitudinal follow-up are also needed to verify learning outcomes and provide a more robust empirical basis for the design and application of LLM-based intelligent tutoring systems.

items.title: From law to practice: model-level operationalization of technical governance requirements for high-risk AI in healthcare
items.abstract: The European Union published the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) in a strategic effort to align the development and application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the common market. This act, one of the first laws of its kind, strengthened the development of trustworthy and human-centered AI through new regulations, prescribing requirements that providers of AI systems must conform to. The Act prescribes model-level technical requirements for high-risk AI systems, such as in terms of accuracy, robustness and fairness, which are to be addressed and reported in the form of conformity assessments. We identify, however, a significant gap between the high-level legal descriptions provided in the law and the low-level requirements needed for the implementation of automated assessment tools for algorithmic auditing. This gap is a major obstacle in the operationalization of AI Act compliance. The difficulties are aggravated due the lack of harmonized AI standards and the existing heterogeneity of AI models, datasets, and tasks. To address this gap, we present an open-source proof-of-concept assessment tool to operationalize the technical requirements of the AI Act according to the current regulatory landscape. With this tool, we demonstrate a bottom-up interpretation of the technical requirements of the AI Act for an automated evaluation of accuracy, robustness, and fairness. We apply our work to two neural network-based healthcare applications and discuss the requirements for further integration to initial conformity assessment and to extended application to post-market monitoring and other algorithmic auditing frameworks. With further work, the base structure presented here can be applied for integration beyond healthcare to other AI high-risk application domains.

items.title: FROM LINGUISTIC ANALYSIS TO AI-ENHANCED PEDAGOGY: PREPARING 21ST-CENTURY LANGUAGE TEACHERS FOR CRITICAL, CONTEXT-AWARE LEARNING
items.abstract: The integration of linguistics and digital educational technologies requires more than adding artificial intelligence (AI) tools to existing language lessons. It requires teachers who can connect linguistic knowledge, pedagogical design, critical evaluation, and responsible technology use. This article proposes a practical framework for AI-supported language teaching in which linguistic analysis becomes the basis for meaningful, context-sensitive learning. The study uses a conceptual and analytical approach, drawing on research into AI in language education, international guidance on teacher AI competencies, and an illustrative teaching sequence built around intertextuality - the way a text draws meaning from other texts and cultural references. The framework includes five stages: identify a language phenomenon, contextualise its function, generate AI-supported alternatives, verify outputs against reliable sources, and evaluate learning through a learner-produced task. The article argues that AI is most educationally valuable when it supports inquiry and feedback rather than replacing teachers’ judgement or learners’ interpretive work. It also outlines risks involving inaccurate explanations, cultural flattening, privacy, bias, and overdependence. The proposed model offers teacher educators a transferable structure for integrating linguistic content with digital tools while maintaining human agency, academic integrity, and clear learning outcomes.

items.title: From Multimodal Observables to Latent Trustiness: Mathematical Modeling of Human Trust in AI Interaction
items.abstract: Continuous assessment of human trust in artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally a latent-state identification problem: trust cannot be observed directly, while its behavioral manifestations are noisy, multimodal, and often shared with other internal states such as cognitive load, uncertainty, and attention. This work introduces trustiness as an operational latent variable for characterizing the time-varying trust-related state of a user interacting with an AI system. Rather than treating behavioral measurements as direct proxies for trust, we formulate their relationship with trustiness within a multimodal state-space framework that explicitly separates latent trust, cognitive load, contextual factors, and noisy observations. Candidate gaze, head-motion, and interaction-derived features are characterized through marginal, conditional, and incremental mutual information to determine which observables retain trust-related information after accounting for confounding and multimodal redundancy. The resulting informative observation set is integrated into a recursive latent-state estimator, instantiated through an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for continuous inference. In a controlled study with 60 participants, gaze entropy, revisit behavior, verification actions, response latency, and inspection time provided the strongest independent trust-related evidence, while conditioning on cognitive load substantially reduced several otherwise apparent associations. The selected multimodal model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.112, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.149, and a Pearson correlation of 0.79 with self-reported trust across all 60 participants, evaluated on post-calibration interactions after participant-specific Trustiness Calibration Experiment (TCE) calibration. Participants were held out from population-level feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. Calibration was conclusive for 57 of 60 participants, for whom the corresponding MAE was 0.108, RMSE was 0.143, and Pearson correlation was 0.81. Joint modeling of trustiness and cognitive load reduced MAE by 18.2% relative to a trustiness-only model in the conclusive-calibration evaluation, while conditional feature selection improved generalization compared with the complete unfiltered observation set. Temporal experiments further showed coherent degradation and recovery of the inferred latent state following controlled changes in AI reliability. These results indicate that continuous trust assessment is better formulated as the identification of a partially observable latent state from confounded multimodal evidence than as direct prediction from behavioral proxies, providing a mathematical framework for multimodal trust estimation in human–AI interaction.

items.title: From Placement to Practice: A Two-Phase Interaction Design Study of Smartphone Video See-Through Stylus Interaction
items.abstract: Smartphone video see-through (VST) stylus interaction could support digital ink input on everyday surfaces, reducing reliance on specialised hardware and small screens. Yet the user experience of these systems is not well understood. Unlike writing on paper, users must coordinate a stylus, surface, and display while managing occlusion, stability, surface access, and comfort. We examine user experience through a two-phase study of smartphone VST stylus use. A participatory placement study identified how users intuitively position the phone, stylus, and surface, revealing the handheld position as the most preferred. A usability evaluation of a handheld prototype showed that overall participants found the system to be intuitive to use, with high usability and low workload. These results indicate that stylus VST interaction is a promising way forward for accessible, large-scale, freeform digital input. We contribute design implications for future stylus VST systems including stable repositioning, stylus-position feedback, tracing support, training and ergonomics.

items.title: From Prefabricated Content to Situated Generation: A Four-Wave Longitudinal Study of AI-Mediated Museum Surfaces and Spaces
items.abstract: Generative AI changes a basic condition of interactive surfaces and spaces (ISS): visitor-facing content can be produced during interaction rather than fully authored before it. We report a longitudinal qualitative study with 23 Chinese science museum practitioners, interviewed annually from 2023 to 2026 (retention 23 to 19) and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants’ accounts moved from anticipated epistemic and operational risks, through backstage experimentation and visitor-facing trials, toward situated governance and renewed questions about the purpose of museum interaction. Following these changes over time shows how generative AI reconfigured the design problems of museum ISS: generated content appeared under institutional authority; inference delay became publicly and bodily experienced; concurrent touch, gesture, and speech created ambiguous multi-user intent; and post-generation editing could leave curators selecting within an AI-defined possibility space. We conceptualize the resulting shift as a movement from prefabricated display to situated generation and formulate four design propositions concerning provenance at the point of display, spatially appropriate fallback, multi-intent negotiation, and curatorial control before generation. These propositions are grounded in practitioner accounts rather than evaluations of implemented solutions.
